title: Where are you from?
goal: Say where you're from, where you live, and which languages you speak — and see for the first time that place names CHANGE FORM after a preposition, and that English "where" covers three separate Slovenian question words.
bekal: ask and answer *Od kod si?* and *Kje živiš?*
name a country, its people, and its language — three different words from one root
recognize *iz + rodilnik* and *v + mestnik* as memorized chunks, before the rules are taken apart in units 6 and 8

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Na hodniku pred predavalnico
dialogs.intro: In a university hallway, before a lecture starts. Budi has been in Ljubljana for just two weeks; Luka is a second-year student.

lines.speaker: Luka:
lines.id: I see! And where do you live now?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zdaj živim v Ljubljani. Pa ti?
lines.id: Now I live in Ljubljana. And you?
lines.literal: now I-live in Ljubljana. and you?

lines.speaker: Luka:
lines.text: Jaz sem iz Maribora, zdaj pa študiram tukaj.
lines.id: I'm from Maribor, but now I study here.
lines.literal: I am from Maribor, now but I-study here.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Which language do you speak at home?

lines.speaker: Luka:
lines.id: Slovenian, of course. And a little German.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Very little. I'm only just starting.

notes: **Three question words for one "where".** English uses "where" for everything and just tacks on extras: *where*, *where to*, *where from*. Slovenian has three separate whole words: **kje** (where — location), **kam** (where to), **od kod** (where from). Picking the wrong one isn't just a bit sloppy — the sentence ends up asking something else.

**Place names change form, and it's obligatory.** Look closely: *Indonezija* becomes *iz Indonezije*, *Jakarta* becomes *iz Jakarte*, *Maribor* becomes *iz Maribora*, and *Ljubljana* becomes *v Ljubljani*. This isn't style, it's **sklon** (case) — a system of endings that does much of the work English leaves to prepositions and word order. For now, learn each pair as one chunk; the rules get unpacked slowly from unit 6 on.

**Languages are said with an adverb, not a noun.** *Govorim slovensko* is literally "I speak Slovenian-ly". The noun exists — *slovenščina* — but it's used for other things: *Učim se slovenščino* ("I'm learning Slovenian"). With *govoriti*, always use the *-o* form: *slovensko, angleško, nemško, indonezijsko*.

**Pa — the little word that adapts.** In this one dialogue *pa* turns up three times with three flavors: *Pa ti?* = "and you?", *zdaj pa študiram* = "but now I study", *Slovensko pa?* = "and what about Slovenian?". It never stands at the start of a sentence and has no fixed translation — it signals that the conversation is turning. Get a feel for it first; don't memorize a meaning.
**Seveda.** It means "of course" and is used exactly like that. It's one of the words you'll hear most in Slovenia; its partners *žal* (unfortunately) and *mogoče* (maybe) follow in unit 19.

grammars.title: Present-tense verbs — nine forms, one pattern
body: Slovenian verbs change according to who is doing the action, like other European languages — the difference is that there are nine slots, not six, because the dual lane joins in. Here is *govoriti* (to speak), whose pattern holds for hundreds of other verbs.
after: Notice that the endings — *-m, -š, -∅, -va, -ta, -ta, -mo, -te, -jo* — are the same for almost every Slovenian verb. Only the vowel in front changes: *govor**i**m* but *del**a**m* (I work) and *ber**e**m* (I read).

Because the ending already tells you who's acting, **the pronoun can be dropped**: *Govorim slovensko* can only mean "I speak Slovenian". So drop it; saying *jaz* over and over sounds like you're defending yourself.

grammars.title: Iz + rodilnik: saying where you're from
body: The preposition *iz* (from) makes the next noun change form. If the place name ends in **-a**, swap it for **-e**; if it ends in a consonant, add **-a**. Those two lines already cover most country and city names.
after: The *Bali* row shows one small thing that often confuses people: *iz* becomes **z** before certain sounds, purely to make it easier to say. The full rule is in unit 18; for now, just follow what's in the table.

This *-e* form is called the **rodilnik** (Genitive) — the second of six cases. It isn't only used after *iz*: it also shows possession (*hiša moje mame* = my mom's house) and appears after numbers from five up (unit 5). You'll meet it constantly.

grammars.title: Kje živiš? — v + mestnik
body: To say where you live, Slovenian uses *v* (in) or *na* (on/at), and the place name changes again — this time into a form called the **mestnik** (Locative).
after: The sound pattern is easy to remember: the **-i** ending for feminine words (*Ljubljan**a*** → *v Ljubljan**i***), and **-u** for masculine words (*Maribor* → *v Maribor**u***).

Why *v Ljubljani* but *na Baliju*? Because islands, mountains, and squares take *na*, while cities and countries take *v*. Part of the choice makes sense, part of it is just habit — and the full list is waiting in unit 8.

blocks.text: From one root, Slovenian grows four words: the country, the word for a man, the word for a woman, and the language form. English gets by with fewer — "a German speaks German in Germany" — so this part really does need memorizing.
Notice that country names take a **capital letter**, while the language form is **lowercase**: *Slovenija* but *slovensko*. Words for people are capitalized too: *Slovenec*, *Indonezijka*.

Four country names in this table end in *-ska* or *-ška* — *Hrvaška, Madžarska, Kitajska, Japonska*. That form is really an adjective frozen into a name, and it changes like an adjective: *iz Hrvaške*, *na Hrvaškem* (in Croatia). For now, just memorize the *iz* form.

blocks.title: A neat little trap
items: People from **Avstrija** speak **nemško**, not "avstrijsko". Language and nationality don't always pair up — just like Americans speaking *angleško*.
And be careful to tell **Avstrija** (Austria) from **Avstralija** (Australia). The two are neighbors in the dictionary, not on the map, and thousands of learners mix them up every year.

sections.title: Kje, kam, od kod — three roads for one "where"

blocks.text: Slovenian sorts place questions by **direction of movement**: staying put, heading there, or coming from there. Each choice drags along its own prepositions and its own noun form.

Watch one city name pass through those three rows: *Ljubljan**i*** → *Ljubljan**o*** → *Ljubljan**e***. Same noun, three different endings. This is the real reason Slovenian has six cases: **the preposition alone isn't enough to make the meaning clear**, so the noun pitches in.
The good news is that this sorting is logical and consistent. After ten uses, your hand picks the ending on its own without you thinking — and from then on, Slovenian stops feeling like a table.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with the right form after iz.
Fill in the blanks with the right form of govoriti.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Od kod si? — Iz Indonezije sem. — Zdaj živim v Ljubljani. — Govorim indonezijsko in angleško. — Maja je iz Maribora. — Ne govorim nemško.
